big_idea: A handful of specific, ordinary-seeming words, used deliberately and paired with genuine relationship-building, can measurably shift how motivated, connected, and cooperative other people feel, because each triggers a well-documented psychological response.

tool.label: The Because Justification Trigger
tool.text: Adding the word because plus any reason, even a weak one, before a request substantially increases compliance, since people respond to the presence of a justification more than to its actual logical strength. David ties this to the classic Ellen Langer copier-line study and applies it to workplace requests, delegation asks, and sales language.
tool.note: The underlying research predates the book by decades; David's contribution is packaging it as one of seven practical everyday words rather than originating the finding.

ideas.title: Yes
ideas.text: Getting a small, genuine yes early in an interaction builds momentum and psychological consistency toward a bigger yes later.

ideas.title: But
ideas.text: What follows but carries the real weight of a sentence in the listener's mind, so reordering critique-then-praise into praise-then-but changes what people actually remember.

ideas.title: Someone's Name
ideas.text: Using a person's name activates automatic attention, making them feel individually seen rather than addressed as part of a group.

ideas.title: If
ideas.text: Framing a request as a hypothetical lowers defensiveness and lets people explore an idea without feeling cornered.

ideas.title: Help
ideas.text: Asking someone for help, rather than assigning a task, activates their sense of competence and social value, increasing engagement.

ideas.title: Thanks
ideas.text: Specific, timely gratitude reinforces the exact behavior you want repeated and strengthens the relationship at low cost.

try_it: In your next request, add a because clause, even a minor one, and notice whether compliance feels easier to get.
Rewrite one piece of feedback this week so praise comes first and any but critique comes second.
Use a colleague's or family member's name explicitly the next time you need their attention in a conversation or email.
Replace one task assignment this week with a request framed as can you help me with.
best_for: Managers, salespeople, and communicators wanting small, immediately testable language tweaks
Readers who like short, actionable chapters over dense theory
less_useful: Readers wanting a rigorous academic treatment of persuasion research, since this is a practical, popular guide
The techniques are interpersonal micro-tactics rather than a strategic influence framework
